_comment: The writing queue, in publication order. The scheduled writing run takes the first entries with status 'pending', writes them, and flips them to 'written'. Dates are assigned at write time by tools/next_slots.py so the schedule stays correct however far behind or ahead it gets.

posts.title: The Great Gods of Samothrace
posts.angle: An initiation open to anyone, on a remote island, whose gods we cannot even reliably name. Philip II met Olympias there. The Nike of Samothrace came from the sanctuary.

posts.title: The Bacchanalia Affair of 186 BCE
posts.angle: Livy's lurid account versus the surviving bronze decree. The Senate legislated against organisation, not debauchery. Cross-link to the pillar and to the Villa of the Mysteries.

posts.title: Isis in Rome: The Goddess Who Travelled
posts.angle: Repeatedly banned by the Republic, embraced by emperors. Apuleius Book 11 as the only initiation narrative. Why an Egyptian goddess out-competed local ones.

posts.title: The Seven Grades of Mithraism
posts.angle: Raven to Father, each tied to a planet. The Ostia mosaic and the Santa Prisca inscriptions. What a promotion ladder implies about a teaching syllabus we have lost entirely.

posts.title: Binding Spells and the Ancient Courtroom
posts.angle: Judicial curse tablets ask for one thing above all: that the opponent be unable to speak. What that reveals about how Greek and Roman trials were actually won.

posts.title: The Evil Eye in the Ancient World
posts.angle: Phallic amulets on doorways, the fascinum worn by children, Pliny on spitting. An anxiety so widespread it shaped domestic architecture.

posts.title: Necromancy in Greece and Rome
posts.angle: From Odysseus at the pit to the recipes in the magical papyri. Legal, illegal, and imperial — emperors consulted the dead and then banned others from doing it.

posts.title: Magical Gems: The Other Half of Ancient Medicine
posts.angle: Thousands of carved gemstones prescribing themselves for stomach pain, childbirth and eye disease, cut with gods and unpronounceable words. Physicians and gem-cutters treated the same complaints and nobody thought that strange. Links to the magical papyri and the curse tablets. Deliberately NOT about envy or the evil eye, which the evil-eye post already covers.

posts.title: The Two Thousand Books Augustus Burned
posts.angle: 12 BCE: the pontifex maximus collects and destroys every unauthorised prophetic book in Rome, keeps the licensed one, edits it, and moves it next to his own house.

posts.title: The Liber Linteus: A Book That Survived as Bandages
posts.angle: The longest surviving Etruscan text reached us wrapped around an Egyptian mummy. A ritual calendar we can read aloud and cannot understand.

posts.title: Why We Still Cannot Read Etruscan
posts.angle: Not a script problem — a language problem. No relatives, no bilinguals of length, and a surviving corpus that is almost entirely gravestones.

posts.title: The Emperor Who Wrote Twenty Books on the Etruscans
posts.angle: Claudius had native speakers, a practising priesthood, state resources, twenty books of research and an endowed annual reading at Alexandria. Every word is gone, and nobody burned it. NOTE: retitled at write time - Suetonius records the Tyrrhenica but mentions no dictionary, and no ancient source does.

posts.title: Delphi: What the Pythia Actually Did
posts.angle: Strip the Victorian imagery. A woman on a tripod, answering yes-or-no questions from states about colonies and wars, with a queue and a fee structure.

posts.title: The Gases Under Delphi
posts.angle: Plutarch describes a sweet-smelling vapour; geologists found intersecting faults and traces of ethylene. Companion piece to the kykeon post — same argument, same honest verdict.

posts.title: Dream Incubation at Epidaurus
posts.angle: Sleep in the sanctuary and the god operates on you in a dream. The inscribed cure testimonies are the strangest medical records to survive antiquity.

posts.title: Reading Lightning: The Etruscan Fulgural Doctrine
posts.angle: Sixteen regions of sky, each with an owner, and a legal procedure for burying a lightning strike. Direct sequel to the Piacenza Liver.

posts.title: The Buried Books of Numa Pompilius
posts.angle: 181 BCE, the Janiculum: farmers dig up two stone chests, one holding Numa's bones, the other his writings. The Senate lets the bones stay buried and burns the books as a threat to state religion. Direct companion to the Augustus post: two burnings for opposite stated reasons. Links to books-augustus-burned and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Chickens That Sank a Roman Fleet
posts.angle: 249 BCE: a consul asks the sacred chickens for the auspices before Drepana, they refuse to eat, he throws them overboard and loses the fleet. What Roman augury actually was as a technical civic office, distinct from Etruscan haruspicy. Links to etruscan-lightning-doctrine, delphi-pythia and piacenza-liver-etruscan.

posts.title: Cybele's Blood Bath: The Roman Taurobolium
posts.angle: 204 BCE: Rome ships in a black stone on Sibylline orders and calls it the Mother of the Gods, while self-castrated Galli parade in the streets. The same Senate crushed the Bacchanalia eighteen years later. Links to cult-of-isis-rome, bacchanalia-186-bce and mithraism-seven-grades.

posts.title: The Sacred Law of Andania
posts.angle: A 92 BCE inscription of 194 lines regulates the mysteries of Andania in more procedural detail than any Greek mystery cult except Eleusis: seating, dress, fines. Revived by a hierophant named Mnasistratos for reasons the text never explains. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and samothrace-great-gods.

posts.title: The Cabeirion: Thebes's Other Mystery Cult
posts.angle: A sanctuary near Thebes where initiates left cups painted with grotesque parodies of the Trojan War, mocking the heroic tradition Thebes claimed descent from. Herodotus calls the rites unspeakable and leaves it there. A deliberately different Great Gods cult from Samothrace. Links to samothrace-great-gods and villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes.

posts.title: 396 CE: The Night the Mysteries Ended
posts.angle: Alaric's Goths burn the sanctuary at Eleusis months after Theodosius had already outlawed the rites. The best witness, Eunapius, had been initiated by the last legitimate hierophant himself. Direct sequel to the Eleusinian Mysteries post. Links to eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion and eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.

posts.title: The Novelist Who Was Tried for Witchcraft
posts.angle: 158 CE, Sabratha: Apuleius stands trial for using magic to seduce a rich widow and defends himself by giving the court a seminar on what real magic looks like. The Apologia is the only complete ancient magic-trial defence to survive. Links to greek-magical-papyri and cult-of-isis-rome.

posts.title: Curse the Charioteer: Magic at the Circus
posts.angle: More than fifty lead tablets from Carthage and Hadrumetum name specific horses and drivers by team colour, calling on demons to break their legs before the race starts, some sharing identical magical formulas. Links to ancient-curse-tablets, ancient-binding-spells-law and evil-eye-ancient-world.

posts.title: The Doll in the Jar: A Love Spell from Egypt
posts.angle: A clay figurine of a bound, kneeling woman, pierced with thirteen needles, found with the lead tablet recipe it was built to follow almost exactly. A fourth-century magician working from a cookbook. Links to greek-magical-papyri and ancient-curse-tablets.

posts.title: The Palladium: Rome's Locked-Room Talisman
posts.angle: A wooden statue only the Vestals and the pontifex maximus could see, sealed in an inner room, said to have come from Troy with Aeneas. A fire in 241 BCE forced Metellus to go in and grab it anyway, and the sources disagree what it cost him. Links to sibylline-books-rome and damnatio-memoriae.

posts.title: The Etruscan Books of the Underworld
posts.angle: The third branch of Etruscan sacred literature: instructions for turning a soul immortal through specific blood sacrifices, quoted only by a hostile Christian polemicist centuries after Etruscan had died as a spoken language. Sequel to the lightning and liver posts. Links to etruscan-lightning-doctrine, piacenza-liver-etruscan and liber-linteus.

posts.title: Pergamon: The Library Built to Beat Alexandria
posts.angle: A royal library built to outdo Alexandria, allegedly starved of papyrus by an Egyptian export ban, which is the origin story told for parchment. Plutarch says Antony later gave the whole collection to Cleopatra, a claim every modern historian who repeats it also flags as unverifiable. Links to library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost and claudius-etruscan-history.

posts.title: The Well That Answered in Oak
posts.angle: At Praeneste the future came out of a well on strips of oak drawn by a child, and in 241 BCE a consul was legally forbidden to consult it. Cicero says only ordinary people ever trusted it, the same century the state trusted the augurs implicitly. Links to delphi-pythia and piacenza-liver-etruscan.

posts.title: Dodona: The Oracle That Answered Everybody
posts.angle: More than four thousand lead strips from Zeus's oldest oracle, most asking not about war or colonies but whose baby a wife is carrying, or whether to take up sheep-farming. Delphi answered states; Dodona answered everybody. Links to delphi-pythia and dream-incubation-asclepius.

posts.title: The Cave They Found Under Virgil's Directions
posts.angle: In 1932 an archaeologist tunnelled into a hillside above Naples and found a 131-metre trapezoidal gallery that matches Virgil's description of the Sibyl's cave closely enough to unnerve people, and still can't be proven to be the actual site. Links to delphi-pythia and sibylline-books-rome.

posts.title: The Oracle That Took Your Smile Away
posts.angle: Consultants at Lebadeia climbed feet-first into a hole in the ground and came out, by multiple accounts, unable to laugh for weeks. Pausanias underwent it himself and wrote up the procedure. Links to dream-incubation-asclepius and oracle-of-the-dead-ephyra.
